232.title: What contemplation is
232.hook: a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus, being with God rather than thinking about him (CCC 2715)
232.carry: I look at him, he looks at me
232.howItsDone: Many Catholics practice silent prayer before the Blessed Sacrament in Eucharistic adoration, sitting in a church or chapel simply to be with Christ, often for an hour at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, risen: an empty tomb, and he goes before you. Today camp five begins, the depths, with how to pray without words.

Every day, an old farmer would stop in the village church and sit there a long time. Not moving his lips, not reading, not holding beads. Just sitting, looking toward the tabernacle. People noticed. This was Ars, a little French village in the 1800s, and the parish priest was John Vianney, now a saint. He finally asked the farmer what he did all that time, and the answer was so simple that the Catholic Church put it in its Catechism. Today's word is what he was doing.
screen: `AN OLD FARMER, SITTING, LOOKING.` → `A VILLAGE IN FRANCE, THE 1800S.` → `WHAT DO YOU DO ALL THAT TIME?`

segments.voice: First, the farmer's answer. As the story is told, he said: I look at him, and he looks at me. No technique. No words. Two people looking at each other. The Catechism calls contemplation a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus, and tells this story to explain it. Second, the word itself. Contemplation comes from Latin, and inside it is templum, the same root as temple. A templum was a patch of sky or ground marked out by Roman priests for watching carefully. To contemplate was to mark out a space and look, with full attention. Catholics took the word and pointed it at God. Third, how it's different. Catholics describe three expressions of prayer. Vocal prayer uses words: the Our Father, the rosary. Meditation uses the mind: you think about a Gospel scene and turn it over. Contemplation is simpler: being with God rather than thinking about him. Saint Teresa of Avila, a Spanish nun of the 1500s, described it as time spent alone with the one we know loves us, like close friends. With a close friend, you don't need to talk the whole time. Fourth, a psalm from camp four says it in one line. In the Douay-Rheims: "Be still and see that I am God." The Church teaches that contemplation isn't just for monks and nuns. It's a gift God can give anyone, in a kitchen or a car or a pew. The farmer from Ars had no degree and no method. He just showed up, and looked.
screen: `I LOOK AT HIM, HE LOOKS AT ME.` · `TEMPLUM: A SPACE MARKED OUT TO WATCH.` · `WORDS, THEN THOUGHT, THEN GAZE.` · `NOT ONLY FOR MONKS.` · then, large: `BE STILL AND SEE THAT I AM GOD.`

segments.voice: Place a crucifix or an icon in front of you for a minute or longer, or if you don't have one, a picture on your phone, a candle, or simply the sky through a window. Don't try to think anything about it; just look, and when your mind wanders, and it will, come back to looking. If you pray, you can let yourself be looked at in return, the way the farmer did; if you don't, just rest in seeing one thing fully.
Contemplation. A gaze of faith: being with God rather than thinking about him. Today's word.
Your line: I look at him, he looks at me. No words needed. That's day two hundred thirty-two.

233.title: Lectio divina, 1: read
233.hook: the monks' ladder of four steps; first, read a short passage slowly
233.howItsDone: Catholics practice lectio divina with the day's Mass readings, alone or in parish groups, reading a short passage slowly several times before moving on to meditation, prayer and quiet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, contemplation: the old farmer of Ars, who said I look at him, he looks at me. Today, a ladder that climbs toward that gaze, one rung at a time.
screen: `I LOOK AT HIM, HE LOOKS AT ME.`

segments.voice: One day a Carthusian monk named Guigo was busy with work for his hands, and he started thinking about the inner work monks do. All at once, he says, four steps came to mind. He wrote them down in a short letter to a brother monk named Gervase, and pictured them as a ladder: its foot on the ground, its top piercing the clouds. The first rung is the simplest: read. But slowly. Not the way a thumb skims a screen, half a headline on the way to the next thing. Slowly enough to taste the words.
screen: `GUIGO, AT WORK WITH HIS HANDS.` → `FOUR STEPS COME TO MIND.` → `A LADDER THROUGH THE CLOUDS.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Lectio divina is Latin for divine reading, or holy reading. Monks practiced it long before Guigo: Saint Benedict's Rule sets aside hours of the day for holy reading. Guigo's gift was to describe its steps. Second, the ladder. Four rungs: reading, meditation, prayer, contemplation, one a day for four days. He sums them up, roughly: reading seeks, meditation finds, prayer asks, contemplation tastes. It echoes Jesus in the Douay-Rheims: "Ask, and it shall be given you: seek, and you shall find: knock, and it shall be opened to you." Third, what reading means here. Not a lot. A little, slowly, more than once: a single verse, a few lines at most. Benedict's Rule even asks anyone reading in the rest hour not to disturb the others, a hint that reading made a sound. Mouth and ears joined the eyes. Guigo compares it to putting food in your mouth: you're not eating yet, but you've taken a bite. Fourth, what to read. Some take the day's Gospel from Mass, or a psalm. One verse rides up all four rungs here, so you can climb with it: Jesus in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, "Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you." That's the whole reading. Reading slowly is the opposite of scrolling: you're not looking for the next thing. You're staying with this one.
screen: `LECTIO DIVINA: HOLY READING.` · `READ, MEDITATE, PRAY, CONTEMPLATE.` · `A LITTLE, SLOWLY, HALF ALOUD.` · `ONE VERSE FOR ALL FOUR RUNGS.` · then, large: `COME TO ME, ALL YOU THAT ARE BURDENED.`

segments.voice: Say the verse quietly, under your breath: come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Say it again, slower, then a third time, and notice which word catches; don't explain it yet, that's tomorrow. Whether you pray or not, reading slowly is the whole job today.
Lectio divina. Latin for holy reading: a short passage, read slowly, the first rung of the monks' ladder. Today's word.
Your line: read slowly. It's the first rung of four. Day two hundred thirty-three, done.

234.title: Lectio divina, 2: meditate
234.hook: chew on one word the way a cow chews the cud
234.howItsDone: In Catholic tradition, meditation means reflecting on a passage of Scripture or a mystery of faith with mind, imagination and heart, often during the rosary or after the day's Gospel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lectio divina, the first rung: read slowly, with the verse come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Today, the second rung.

If you've ever driven past a field of cows, you've seen them lying there, jaws going round and round for what seems like hours. They're not eating anything new. They're chewing the cud: bringing back up what they already ate and chewing it again, to get the good out of it. It doesn't sound like a picture of prayer. But monastic writers borrowed it for exactly that: a word read once, brought back, and chewed again. That's the second rung.
screen: `COWS IN A FIELD, CHEWING.` → `BRINGING IT BACK UP, AGAIN.` → `THE MONKS BORROWED THIS PICTURE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Meditatio is Latin for meditation. In Catholic prayer, meditation doesn't mean emptying your mind. It means filling it with one thing and turning it over. The monks had another name for it, ruminatio, rumination, from the Latin for chewing the cud. Guigo, who described the ladder, says reading puts the food in your mouth, and meditation chews it and breaks it down. Second, the root. Back in camp four, Psalm 1 had a day of its own. In the Douay-Rheims, the blessed man is the one whose "will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he shall meditate day and night." The Hebrew word behind meditate is hagah, to murmur, the sound of a lion growling over its catch. Meditation holds on to a word and won't let go. Third, the model. Catholic writers point to Mary. After the shepherds came at Christmas, Luke says: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." She didn't understand everything. She kept it, and kept turning it. Fourth, how it works with the verse. Take the word that caught you yesterday and ask it questions. Burdened: what am I carrying? Since when? Come: come where, and how? Refresh: what would that feel like? You're not studying it like a textbook. You're letting it meet your actual life. The Catechism says meditation engages thought, imagination, emotion and desire: your whole self, chewing one small word.
screen: `MEDITATIO: CHEW IT OVER.` · `PSALM 1: MURMUR IT DAY AND NIGHT.` · `MARY KEPT THESE WORDS, PONDERING.` · `ASK YOUR WORD QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `ON HIS LAW HE SHALL MEDITATE DAY AND NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Say the verse once more: come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Pick one word, come, or burdened, or refresh, or whichever caught you, and say it slowly on your breath, again and again, letting it ask you a question about your own day. Don't hurry to an answer; if you pray, do this in God's presence.
Meditatio. Latin for meditation: the second rung, chewing on one word from the reading, turning it over, letting it meet your life. Today's word.
Your line: chew the word. Reading takes the bite, and meditation chews. See you on the next rung.

235.title: Lectio divina, 3: pray
235.hook: answer God with what the word stirred up
235.howItsDone: In lectio divina Catholics move from reading and reflecting to speaking to God in their own words about what the passage stirred, and in the Mass the congregation answers each reading with a response.

segments.voice: Yesterday, meditatio, the second rung: chewing one word the way a cow chews the cud. Today, the third rung: you answer.

A long, careful letter arrives from someone who loves you. You read it slowly. You read it again. You think about it all day. And then you never write back. Not a word. Put like that, it sounds strange. Yet it's easy to treat Scripture that way: read it, maybe think about it, close the book. Guigo's ladder has a third step, the one that turns reading into a conversation. You answer.
screen: `A LETTER FROM SOMEONE WHO LOVES YOU.` → `AND YOU NEVER WRITE BACK.` → `THE THIRD STEP: ANSWER.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Oratio is Latin for prayer, but also for a speech; English gets oration and oratory from it. It means speaking, out loud or inside, directly to someone. Second, the turn. Reading and meditation are about the word. Prayer talks to the one who spoke it. Guigo says meditation makes the soul see what it lacks, and hunger for it, and then prayer asks. If your word was burdened, and you found you're carrying something heavy, today you tell God about it. Plainly. Third, the model. One picture of it is the boy Samuel in the Temple. God calls his name in the night, three times, and he keeps running to the old priest Eli. Finally Eli tells him how to answer, and Samuel says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth." God speaks first; prayer is the reply. Fourth, what kind of answer. Not a polished speech. Whatever the word stirred up. Thanks, if it was comfort. Sorrow, if it showed you something wrong. A request, if it showed you a need. Even a complaint: plenty of psalms argue with God, and the Church prays them in its daily prayer. Remember the father in Mark who cried help my unbelief? One sentence, with tears. That counts. The Catechism describes prayer as a living relationship, God's thirst meeting the human thirst for God. Lectio divina gives that relationship something to talk about.
screen: `ORATIO: PRAYER, AND SPEECH.` · `FROM THE WORD TO THE ONE WHO SPOKE.` · `SPEAK, LORD, SAMUEL ANSWERS.` · `THANKS, SORROW, ASKING, COMPLAINT.` · then, large: `SPEAK, LORD, FOR THY SERVANT HEARETH.`

segments.voice: Say the verse once more: come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Go back to your word and what it stirred up these two days, and answer with one honest sentence, quietly or inside. If you pray, say it to God as simply as you'd say it to a friend; if you don't, say it to the words themselves, or to the quiet, and let the sentence sit there.
Oratio. Latin for prayer and for speech: the third rung, answering back to God with whatever the word stirred up. Today's word.
Your line: answer back. The reply doesn't need to be polished. That's day two hundred thirty-five.

236.title: Lectio divina, 4: rest
236.hook: stop talking and rest in what's been given
236.howItsDone: Catholics who practice lectio divina end it with a few minutes of silence, simply resting in God's presence, and some monasteries and parishes keep times of silent prayer after the readings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, oratio, the third rung: answering the word with one honest sentence. Today, the top of the ladder, where you stop talking.

Late at night, at the end of a long talk between old friends, a moment can come when everything that needed saying has been said. Nobody reaches for a phone. Nobody fills the quiet. Two people just sit together, and the silence isn't empty. A grandparent holding a sleeping baby knows a quiet like that too. Guigo's ladder ends there. After reading, chewing and answering, the fourth rung isn't another thing to do. It's the moment you stop doing.
screen: `THE END OF A LONG TALK.` → `NOBODY FILLS THE QUIET.` → `THE FOURTH RUNG: STOP DOING.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Contemplatio, Latin for contemplation. It came up four days ago, with the farmer at Ars: I look at him, he looks at me. Now you can see where it sits: at the top of Guigo's ladder. Reading seeks, meditation finds, prayer asks, contemplation tastes. Guigo treats it as a rung you can't climb by trying: while the soul is still asking, he says, God interrupts the prayer and comes to meet it. Second, a gift, not an achievement. The Catechism calls contemplation a gift, a grace: it can't be made to happen, only made room for. Read, chew, answer, then be quiet. In Catholic teaching, the rest is God's part. Some days that silence is full. Some days it's just quiet, and that's fine too. Third, the model. Luke tells of two sisters, Martha and Mary, welcoming Jesus. Martha is busy serving; Mary sits at his feet, listening. When Martha complains, Jesus answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "But one thing is necessary. Mary hath chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her." Martha isn't the villain here; the Church honors her as a saint too. But there's a time to sit. Fourth, the verse's last promise: I will refresh you. In Greek, the word means I will give you rest. You came burdened. You read, you chewed, you answered. Now you rest, like the weaned child in the psalm from camp four, quiet against its mother. Not asleep. Just close, and still.

segments.voice: Say the verse one last time: come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Then stop, and for two minutes sit without words: don't chew, don't answer, don't plan, just sit the way you'd sit with an old friend at the end of the night, and let thoughts pass like cars on a far-off road. If you pray, simply rest in God's company; if you don't, rest in the quiet itself.
Contemplatio. The fourth rung: after reading, chewing and answering, you stop, and rest in what's been given. Today's word.
Your line: rest in it. The top rung isn't climbed; it's given. See you tomorrow.

237.title: The examen
237.hook: Ignatius's daily look back: thanks, light, review, sorrow, hope
237.howItsDone: Many Catholics, especially those formed by the Jesuits, pray the examen once or twice a day, often at night, and an examination of conscience is also how Catholics prepare for confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the top of the ladder: contemplatio, where you stop talking and rest. Lectio divina reads a page of Scripture. Today, a way to read the page of your own day.

In 1521, a young Basque soldier named Iñigo was defending the fortress of Pamplona when a cannonball smashed his leg. Months in bed, bored out of his mind, he asked for adventure novels. The house only had a life of Christ and a book of saints. He read them, and noticed something odd: daydreams of glory left him empty afterward, and daydreams of following Christ left him glad. He'd started paying attention to what was happening inside him. That soldier became Saint Ignatius of Loyola, and the habit became today's word.
screen: `1521: A CANNONBALL AT PAMPLONA.` → `ONLY TWO BOOKS IN THE HOUSE.` → `HE STARTS PAYING ATTENTION.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Examen is Latin, with a lovely old meaning: the needle on a balance scale, the little pointer that shows which way things tip. An examen is a daily look at which way your day tipped. Second, the steps. In his Spiritual Exercises, published in 1548, Ignatius lays out a short daily prayer in five points, often summed up today in five words. Thanks: remember what you were given today. Light: ask God for the grace to see your day clearly and honestly. Review: walk back through it hour by hour, like watching a film. Where was there life? Where did you go wrong? Sorrow: ask forgiveness for what needs it. Hope: look toward tomorrow, and ask for help with it. Third, the order. What comes first isn't your sins. It's thanks. Ignatius puts gratitude before examining anything, and many who teach the examen say that's the secret: you look at your day as someone who has been loved all day long. It's not an audit. It's a conversation about the day with someone who was there. Fourth, why it lasts. Ignatius founded the Jesuits, and the story is often told that he let his companions shorten other prayers when they were busy or sick, but never the examen. Today it's prayed in Jesuit schools, in homes at bedtime, even by people who've never met a Jesuit. It takes ten or fifteen minutes, and at its heart is your line: where was God today?
screen: `EXAMEN: THE NEEDLE ON A SCALE.` · `THANKS, LIGHT, REVIEW, SORROW, HOPE.` · `GRATITUDE COMES FIRST.` · `NEVER SKIP THE EXAMEN.` · then, large: `WHERE WAS GOD TODAY?`

segments.voice: Walk the five steps through today so far: name one thing you're grateful for, ask to see honestly, then run back through the day like a film on fast forward, stopping where you felt most alive and where you felt worst. Name anything that needs forgiving, then think of the rest of today. If you pray, do all five with God; if you don't, do them with honest attention.

238.title: Consolation and desolation
238.hook: what draws you toward God and what drags you away
238.howItsDone: Catholics who make Ignatian retreats or meet with a spiritual director often talk through their consolations and desolations, using Ignatius's rules for the discernment of spirits to make decisions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the examen: Ignatius's five steps, beginning with thanks. Today, the two words Ignatius used for what you find when you look. And the week ends.

Two evenings. On one, the drive home is light: a kind word given or received, and the world seems roomy. On the other, everything's gray, people get snapped at, and praying, or trying at all, looks pointless. It's easy to file these under good days and bad days. Ignatius wouldn't. In his Spiritual Exercises they're more than moods. They're movements, inner pulls with a direction, and he gives them names. Today's word is the first of the two.
screen: `ONE EVENING, LIGHT.` → `ANOTHER, EVERYTHING'S GRAY.` → `NOT MOODS: MOVEMENTS.`

segments.voice: First, consolation, from the Latin for comfort, being comforted. In his Spiritual Exercises, Ignatius describes it as any inner movement that draws the soul toward God: an increase of faith, hope and love, a deep peace, joy that lifts you toward what matters. Second, desolation, the opposite pull: darkness, restlessness, a drift toward low things, feeling lazy, lukewarm, sad, as if cut off from God. Here's the surprise: consolation isn't the same as feeling good. Tears of sorrow for something you've done wrong can be consolation, because they turn you toward God. And a fun, busy week can hide desolation, if it's quietly pulling you away. The question isn't how do I feel. It's which way am I being pulled. Third, the rules. Ignatius gives advice for both, and one rule is blunt: in desolation, never make a change. Don't quit, don't break up, don't move across the country when everything feels dark. Stay with the decisions you made in a better light, pray a little more, and wait; Ignatius expects it to pass. In consolation, enjoy it, give thanks, and store up strength for the harder days. Fourth, what it means. In Ignatius's reading, desolation isn't proof God has left. He says God can allow it, to teach that consolation is a gift, not something anyone manufactures. This week in camp five: contemplation, the four rungs of lectio divina, read, meditate, pray, rest, then the examen, and now consolation. Every one is a way of paying attention.
screen: `CONSOLATION: DRAWN TOWARD GOD.` · `DESOLATION: DRAGGED AWAY.` · `IN DESOLATION, MAKE NO CHANGE.` · `A GIFT, NOT MANUFACTURED.` · then, large: `WHICH WAY AM I BEING PULLED?`

segments.voice: The examen asked where God was; this asks about direction, so go back over the last day and find the moment you felt most drawn toward life, toward love, toward God if you believe: that's your consolation. Then find the moment you felt most pulled away, dragged down, closed in, and name it without judging: that's your desolation. Notice the direction of each, not just the feeling, and if you pray, bring both to God, the high with thanks, the low with honesty.
Consolation. In Ignatius's language, any movement that draws you toward God, even through tears. Its opposite is desolation. Today's word.
Your line: notice the pull. A heavy mood is no time for a big decision. That's the week.
